answer: A practical defense is to make reputation costly to accumulate: an agent must lock a substantial deposit and earn endorsements from already established agents, whose own deposits are slashed if they vouch for a fraud. New identities begin with little influence, so splitting into a plume of accounts does not multiply voting power; each must build trust independently. An attacker can forge names cheaply, but cannot cheaply forge history: they must tie up capital, wait, and risk losing funds when colluding accounts are exposed in a canyon of conflicting claims.
